site.name: Joseph Sherlock
site.tagline: Assistant Professor at King’s College London, behavioral scientist in a public policy school with 12 years’ experience running randomized controlled trials. I focus on using behavioral science as a vehicle to innovate in civic society.
site.bio: Behavioral Scientist with 12 years of experience, specializing in democracy and sustainability, designing and leading large-scale randomized controlled field experiments in complex, real-world settings. Work spans the USA, the UK, and multiple international contexts, partnering with major government bodies, civic organizations, and multilateral institutions. Holds a PhD in Psychological and Behavioural Science from the London School of Economics and Political Science and currently serves as Assistant Professor at the School for Government, King’s College London. Advises the UN Secretary General’s office and teaches short courses for Duke University.
site.quote: Humans haven’t changed much, but the world around us has. I explore how we innovate to help us adapt.

focus.title: Democracy
focus.body: For democracy to survive, we need to innovate. This requires us to experiment. I study how behavioral science can boost civic trust, improve transparency, and make democratic institutions fit for the current world.

focus.title: Sustainability
focus.body: My work applies behavioural insights to encourage sustainable action, helping individuals and institutions close the gap between climate intention and behaviour.

focus.title: Method
focus.body: As we enter our second decade as an applied behavioural science field, it is time we understood more effectively how we do what we do, and what leads to success as an applied behavioural scientist.

featured.title: Politricks
rows: Context
Misinformation threatens democracy and climate action, eroding trust and amplifying polarization.
Problem
Few studies compare active (games) and passive (guides) learning in helping citizens discern manipulative content.
Intervention
We built Politricks, an interactive game, alongside a passive inoculation guide, each teaching three manipulation tactics: emotional storytelling, conformity, and conspiracy theories.
Outcome
Active and passive tools are comparably effective, scalable strategies for building resilience against misinformation.

featured.title: Operational Transparency in Elections
featured.kicker: Preprint · under review at Nature Human Behaviour
rows: Context
Democracies face declining trust fuelled by polarization, misinformation, and hidden election processes.
Problem
Voters often misinterpret how elections work, leading to scepticism and disengagement.
Intervention
Applying behavioural insights to increase operational transparency, redesign ballots for usability, and work with election officials to test communication and procedural reforms.
Outcome
Evidence-based, incremental interventions make democratic systems more understandable and trustworthy, reducing misinformation’s impact and strengthening confidence in elections.

featured.title: COVID-19 Vaccination in Ghana
rows: Context
Ghana faced vaccine hesitancy despite availability, with uptake shaped by social and cultural factors.
Problem
Traditional drivers such as provider recommendations were unexpectedly less predictive; family and religious leaders influenced decisions far more.
Intervention
A two-part study surveyed 1,494 people and tested behaviourally informed message frames (fear, altruism, social norms) delivered through trusted messengers.
Outcome
Tailoring strategies to leverage social trust and context-specific nudges can increase vaccine uptake in Ghana.
